How to choose a gift for a reader

By Couple Better Gifts · Updated October 5, 2026 · How we choose gifts

Someone who loves a fantasy series may want another edition of it, a useful reading accessory, or neither. A crowded shelf, a digital-only habit, and a strong preference for one translation can change the decision. Find out whether they read paper books or an e-reader, and where they usually read.

Find out what they enjoy about reading

A favorite author or character can help you choose a book or collectible. For an accessory, think about where they read and whether they take notes. Ask about the particular gift type: do they collect figures, keep a reading journal, or need a light for reading in bed?

Ask one small question. “Do you like keeping reading notes?” gives you useful evidence for a journal. “Do you usually read print or digital?” can prevent a purchase that has no place in their routine. You can keep the exact gift a surprise while checking the facts that matter.

Reading light: position and comfort first

Think about where the light will sit. A clip-on design depends on something suitable to attach it to. A wearable neck light avoids that attachment but adds weight on the wearer. Consider which position would feel comfortable for them. Look at the dimensions, charging method, controls, and whether the light can be directed where they need it.

Also consider the setting. Someone who reads beside a sleeping partner may want a different light from someone reading at a desk. Product photos often show an ideal arrangement; compare that arrangement with the chair, bed, or book format the recipient actually uses. Check that the beam can reach their pages from that position.

Journal: useful only if it matches their note-taking

A structured reading journal gives prompts and makes entries comparable. A flexible notebook leaves room for longer reactions, sketches, or quotes. The first can feel convenient to one reader and restrictive to another. Look at sample pages before buying.

If they already track books in an app, a journal could duplicate a system they enjoy. Ask whether they’d enjoy keeping a paper journal too. You can still make an accessory meaningful through a note about a book you discussed together, without asking them to maintain a new record.

Books and collectibles: exact details matter

Check which books they own and whether they care about matching a series’ existing editions. Size, binding, cover style, and edition can matter to a collector. An expensive special edition is a weaker choice when you know only the title and nothing about their preferences.

For character merchandise, check the character, maker, licensing claims, and seller carefully. For a series such as The Stormlight Archive, look for merchandise from a maker licensed to use the characters. Check the maker’s own information and the seller before ordering.

Choosing a smaller gift

Choose something that suits the way they read. If you give a journal, write a short note explaining why you thought it might fit, but leave the recipient free to use it differently. If you choose a shelf item, consider the available display space.

Include shipping and tax in your budget. Check the return policy and ask for a gift receipt if available.

The final check

  • Does it suit print, digital, or both?
  • Does it fit the place they read?
  • Would they enjoy using it?
  • Have you confirmed the exact edition, model, or licensed item?
